answers.justification: Among eligible employees, nomination rates (28.6% vs 28.2%) and committee approval rates (73.8% vs 71.0%) are almost the same, and adjusting for eligibility mix predicts a remote rate of 8.2% against 7.6% observed (C1), so in-person favouritism does not explain the gap; E3, C4 and C9 are anecdotal or untallied.

Only 32.4% of remote employees meet the 18-month time-in-level rule, against 73.7% of office staff (C1, E4 3.1), because 215 of 340 remote staff joined after remote hiring opened (C2); applying office rates within each band reproduces nearly all of the gap (C1).
Remote and office staff are spread across job families in similar proportions (about 50/32/18% vs 50/29/21%), and the gap appears inside every family (E1).
The only support is one manager's anecdote (E3) and selected comments (C8); the staffing system cannot show who received stretch or escalation work (C13), and the managers could not count it (E3).
Remote voluntary exit rates are slightly lower than office rates, both overall (10.9% vs 11.6%) and in the first year (14.2% vs 15.0%) (C2).

The raw gap is real (E1, C14), but almost all of it disappears once eligibility is controlled for (C1), and the analyst note says a residual effect of a few points can be neither confirmed nor ruled out, so causation is not established.

Policy 3.1 bars nomination under 18 months in level except by rare exception (E4), which gives the mechanism, and approval rates are about 2% for ineligible staff against about 21% for eligible staff in both groups (C1).
Remote attrition is not higher than office attrition, overall or in the first year (C2).

The rule targets a cause the data do not support (C1). It would effectively shut out about 180 remote staff on home-based contracts from promotion (E2), likely punishing the wrong group, and Larkhaven lacks the desk capacity without reintroducing booking (C15).

The gap comes from comparing headcounts with very different eligibility (E1, C1, C14), so pausing A1 and reporting eligible-to-eligible comparisons, then re-checking the uncertain residual next cycle (C1 analyst note), fits the evidence.
There is no data showing remote staff get less stretch work (C13), so H4 is unconfirmed (E3, C8 are anecdotal) and a structural overhaul is not yet justified.

Remote staff understand promotion criteria less (41% vs 58%, E5), and comments show some did not know about the 18-month rule (C8), so briefings are low-risk and helpful, but they do not address the main reporting error.
C1 (consistent with C2 and E4) is strong enough to decide not to adopt the attendance rule and to fix the reporting, even though a small residual effect remains uncertain.

ambiguousItems: Q6: 'contradicted' is also defensible, because adjusting for eligibility (C1) removes nearly all of the gap; 'association-only' rests on the analyst's note that a residual effect of several points cannot be ruled out.
Q1: 'unknown' is defensible if one gives weight to the uncertain eligible-band residual (C1) and the anecdotes (E3, C4), but H1 claims to explain the gap itself, which C1 largely rules out.
Q12: 'preferred' is defensible given the understanding gap (E5) and remote staff not knowing the 18-month rule (C8).
Q13: whether A2 counts as substantive (holding the proposal and changing reporting) or as evidence-gathering affects the answer.
caseProblems: The C1 title ('by time in current level and work arrangement') clearly points to the confounder, which partly gives away the intended answer, though such a title is realistic for a People Analytics extract.

All figures cross-check: E1 totals match C1 (122/760, 26/340), and C1 nominations and approvals match C4 (203 nominations, 148 approved). C2's 125 remote staff starting before March 2025 fits 110 eligible. No inconsistencies found.
C3 is mildly off-topic, since unrated recent joiners cannot meet E4's rating requirement, but it is consistent with the tenure explanation.

rulings.explanation: R1 claims that working remotely causes a lower chance of promotion. The raw link is real and repeats across years: 7.6% vs 16.1% in E1, and 9.4% vs 15.5% in C14. So 'unknown' does not fit. C1 shows that eligibility mix accounts for most of the gap (8.2% expected vs 7.6% observed), so 'causal' does not fit either. 'Contradicted' would need evidence that counts against the link itself, as C2 does for R3, where there is no association at all. C1 does not do that. Within each band the remaining differences still point in the claimed direction: 20.0% vs 21.1% among eligible staff and 1.7% vs 2.0% among the rest. The analyst note also says the data cannot rule out a true difference of several points in either direction. So C1 counts against location explaining the 8.5-point gap, not against any causal effect existing. That matches 'association-only' (they co-occur, causation not established). The comparison with H1 is consistent: H1 claims favouritism explains the gap, which C1 rules out, whereas R1 makes no claim about size.
rulings.fix: None needed. Optionally, add one sentence to the C1 analyst note: 'The data neither show nor exclude a small direct effect of location.' This would make the R1 reading explicit.

rulings.explanation: H1 is a claim about where the gap comes from: favouritism by managers and the Promotion Committee. C1 tests both stages directly. Nomination rates among eligible staff match (28.2% vs 28.6%), approval rates are close (71.0% vs 73.8%), and exception nominations are similar (6 vs 6 on comparable not-eligible pools). Eligibility mix explains about 93% of the gap. The gate that drives the gap is a policy rule on time in level (E4), not anyone's discretion. Because C1 discriminates between H1 and H2, 'unknown' does not fit. The evidence pointing the other way is weak. E3 and C4 are anecdotes, and C4's comment was explicitly unchecked. C10 uses unadjusted vendor figures. The small, uncertain residual among eligible staff might allow a minor favouritism effect, but it cannot rescue H1's actual claim that favouritism produces the gap. A careful analyst would mark H1 as contradicted.

A4 (briefings) is low-cost and responds to real signals: the understanding gap in E5 (41% vs 58%) and the C8 comment from a remote joiner who did not know the 18-month rule. But the task is to explain the gap and respond to a pending decision. The gap is a mechanical result of eligibility, and briefings do not change anyone's eligibility or promotion outcomes. A4 also does nothing about the harmful rule that is about to be announced, or the misleading dashboard figure. Both are handled only by A2. E5 is not broken down by tenure, so the understanding gap may simply reflect how recently many remote staff joined. C8 is a hand-picked selection of comments. A4 is reasonable but not among the best actions, so 'acceptable' is correct and 'preferred' overstates it.
rulings.fix: None needed. Optionally, reword A4's rationale to note that briefings cannot change eligibility and so do not address the gap or the pending decision.

rulings.explanation: A2 combines a substantive decision with a follow-up check. It halts the attendance rule (a 'no intervention' style decision, which the rules count as substantive) and changes how promotion is reported. The FY2027 re-check is the only evidence-gathering part. C1 is enough to commit to both substantive parts: the raw figure is confounded, and the rule would target something that does not drive the gap. C2 confirms the composition comes from recent hiring. Even if A2 were treated as mere evidence-gathering, the next substantive candidates still point to 'sufficient'. A4 is low-cost and supported by E5 and C8. Declining A1 is clearly justified by C1. The residual uncertainty in the eligible band does not make the decision unsafe, because holding the rule and reporting by eligibility band is low-risk, reversible, and already includes a re-check. 'Insufficient' cannot be defended under any reading.
rulings.fix: None needed. Optionally, change the key's rationale from 'declines the attendance rule' to 'puts the attendance rule on hold', to match A2's wording.
